not_measured: Anything the codegen spike's fragment does not reach. The spike compiles no perform, no handler-stack walk, no host boundary, no continuation capture, no closure and no derived codec, and it frees its values in an arena rather than reference-counting them. Projecting its k onto the whole interpreter share assumes a coverage it did not demonstrate.
What a partially-covering backend is worth. The spike's `solo, trampolined` variant is one point on that curve; no variant compiles a whole request path.

Rungs 1-6 are taken on /health, not /items: a pure call to the /items handler needs a store, and the only one available in process is std.db's memory engine, whose SQL scanner is on no served request path. /items' own decode and encode therefore sit inside the database rung.
The TLS handshake. The tls rung is steady state over connections carrying 32 requests, as ADR 0016 section 1.2 requires.
Multi-core throughput, deliberately: one machine is one core and a process-per-core number would measure an operating system.
Env::lookup's depth sweep, and the writes and copies a response makes.

The ladder's rungs and total are taken on the sequential accept loop rather than the task-per-connection one ADR 0016 section 1.6 pins, and the reason is measured rather than preferred: a spawning service opens a production region for its whole life and the constant memo is refused inside an open region, so the two arenas would be in different regimes — an in-process numerator that memoizes over a served denominator that does not. Both loops are measured; the other one's rows are the labelled offerings, and what the difference costs is in the limits.

The in-Ply loop rungs 2-4 are read off, apart from the endpoint layer. It costs 0.90us an iteration, measured by running the empty loop at two counts, and it cancels between rungs 3 and 4 because both sides of those are loops. It does not cancel between rungs 1 and 2, whose `without` is a bare call, so the endpoint layer carries it: that layer is 1.17us against 0.90us of scaffold, which is the resolution this rung has and not a number to read to two decimals.

As an end-to-end speedup on the served workload: more native builtins, the frame push, Env::lookup, boxing on hot paths, connection and statement reuse, response buffering. ADR 0016 section 2.5 makes an unpriced lever sufficient on its own to keep deferring.

What a route body costs when it is not a constant. `/health`'s whole body is a nullary pure definition, so after the constant memo the endpoint rung is a memo hit; the /items handler over the twin is 562.2us a call against 356.6us for the twin's scan alone, and that difference is the closest thing here to a route body's own cost.

denominators.floor_taken_on: a Rust accept/read/write/close replaying the same 270-byte /items response over plaintext, over connections carrying 32 requests, with no interpreter, no TLS and no database under it
denominators.total_taken_on: /items over postgres over TLS with --trace json, sequential accept, c=1, best of 3 sweeps

alternatives.name: more native builtins
alternatives.what: Fold `read_line`, `is_token`, `trim_ows` and `trim_end` into one native head scan. W2's lever applied to W3's layer, and W2's was 4.8x.
alternatives.cost: Each native builtin grows the trusted computing base `ply hosts` invites a reader to check.

alternatives.name: the frame push
alternatives.what: ADR 0005's four heap allocations per frame push, paid per node the machine suspends inside. The tree-walker runs the same pure request path 2.82x faster than the control-stack machine (machine against treewalk), which bounds what a cheaper frame representation is worth.
alternatives.cost: A cheaper frame representation touches capture, splice and every frame kind.

alternatives.name: Env::lookup
alternatives.what: `crates/ply-eval/src/env.rs` walks an `Rc` chain linearly, so a variable reference costs O(scope depth). No depth sweep was run.
alternatives.cost: An indexed environment touches capture, splice and every frame kind.

alternatives.name: boxing on hot paths
alternatives.what: One /health request allocates 1082 times and 0.128 MB to produce a 107-byte response, counted with a counting global allocator in `w6-alloc`. The size of the lever, not a speedup: nothing was changed to move it.
alternatives.cost: Unboxing or arena-allocating `Value` touches every builtin and every engine.

alternatives.name: caching derived work
alternatives.what: `table()` builds eleven Route records from their pattern strings and costs 1.26us per call; `route_of` calls it on every request and `health` again through `len(table())`. The constant memo evaluates a nullary pure definition once per process, and it has landed: `ply-eval::memo`, CONTRACTS.md.
alternatives.evidence: The shipped service against the same source with every nullary definition of its own given a dead parameter, served alternately by the same binary over postgres over TLS with --trace json at c=1, best of 3. On the sequential accept loop the ladder is read off: /items 657.0us with the memo against 757.7us without it, and /health 273.0us against 486.1us (1.78x). On the task-per-conn loop: /items 1.00x and /health 1.00x — `task.spawn` opens a region for the life of the server and the memo is refused inside one, so a spawning service memoizes nothing.
alternatives.cost: A memo in front of a pure function changes when a route table can be edited, and both engines have to keep it or `--engine both` reports E0503.

alternatives.name: connection and statement reuse
alternatives.what: W4's pool and prepared-statement cache: hit rate, and what a miss costs. W6 did not re-take it.

alternatives.name: response buffering
alternatives.what: Writes per response, and the copies `bytes_concat` and `bytes_slice` make. `Value::Bytes` is `Arc<[u8]>` with no slicing, so a slice copies.

limits.why: A Value holds Rc and a continuation is Rc<Vec<Segment>>, so a Ply task cannot move between OS threads. Throughput scales by processes, not by threads, and every runtime this would be compared against scales by threads.

limits.what: A Ply request costs 38.5x the same syscalls answering the same bytes
limits.why: The floor is a Rust accept/read/write/close replaying the response the service answers. It has no interpreter under it — and, on the /items row, no TLS and no database either, so the multiple is stated with what each side did.
limits.evidence: 658.9us for /items over postgres over TLS with tracing against a 17.1us floor replaying the same 270-byte response; like for like, /health over plaintext is 268.6us against a 17.2us floor replaying its 107-byte response, 15.7x.

limits.what: A service whose accept loop spawns memoizes nothing
limits.why: `task.spawn` opens a production region that stays open for the life of the server, and `Machine::constant` refuses the constant memo inside any open region — so every nullary pure definition is re-evaluated per call on the task-per-connection loop. The rule's stated reason is a `simulate` region's allocation trail, which a production region does not keep.
limits.evidence: Disabling the memo by source substitution costs 1.78x on /health and 1.15x on /items on the sequential loop, and 1.00x and 1.00x on the task-per-conn loop, where there is nothing to disable: /health is 273.0us sequential against 488.7us spawning, on the same service.

limits.what: The in-memory twin is slower than the database it stands in for
limits.why: std.db's memory engine parses its SQL in Ply on every call, and every twin handler clause writes its whole state back through a persistent map.
limits.evidence: In process the twin's /items handler is 562.2us a call and its scan alone is 356.6us of that.

limits.what: --engine both costs more than two runs
limits.why: The divergence guarantee runs the program twice, and the two engines are not the same speed.
limits.evidence: The treewalk runs the pure request path 2.82x faster than the machine.

limits.what: No cancellation, no backpressure, no load shedding
limits.why: ADR 0011 left cancellation unresolved through W5, and W4's promise of backpressure was broken explicitly by W5's `not in` list.

limits.what: A request allocates far more times than it writes bytes
limits.why: Value is boxed, a frame push is four heap allocations, and every intermediate Bytes is an Arc<[u8]>.
limits.evidence: One /health request allocates 1082 times and 0.128 MB to produce a 107-byte response.
